title: Scientists Uncover 165-Million-Year-Old Chinese Fossil With Broad Swimming Tail and Bony Throat】
body:
Scientists have uncovered a 165‑million‑year‑old fossil in western China that reveals a previously unknown mammalian ancestor equipped with a broad, paddle‑like tail and reinforced throat bones—features that suggest an early adaptation to an aquatic lifestyle. The specimen, belonging to a tiny Jurassic mammaliaform, provides fresh insight into how some of the first mammals may have diversified beyond the terrestrial niches traditionally ascribed to them, hinting at a far more complex evolutionary experiment in the age of dinosaurs.

The fossil, unearthed from the Tiaojishan Formation in Liaoning Province, consists of an exceptionally well‑preserved partial skeleton that includes the vertebral column, hind limbs, and a strikingly expanded caudal vertebrae series. Researchers interpreting the remains describe the tail as “broad and flattened,” a morphology reminiscent of modern otters and beavers, whose tails function as powerful rudders for swimming. In addition, the animal possessed a series of ossified hyoid elements—a bony structure supporting the tongue and throat—that are unusually robust for a creature of its size. Together, these traits point to a capability for sustained underwater propulsion and possibly a diet that involved catching small aquatic prey.

The discovery challenges long‑standing assumptions that early mammals were strictly small, nocturnal, and strictly terrestrial, living in the shadows of the dominant dinosaurs. While previous finds have hinted at semi‑aquatic habits in certain Mesozoic mammals—such as the gliding gliriforms and the insect‑eating *Megaconus*—the new specimen provides the most concrete anatomical evidence yet of a true swimming adaptation. “The combination of a broad tail and a reinforced hyoid apparatus is a hallmark of animals that spend a considerable amount of time in water,” said Dr. Li Wei, lead author of the study. “It suggests that this lineage was already experimenting with niche partitioning that would later be seen in fully aquatic mammals like whales and seals, albeit on a much smaller scale.”

The fossil’s age places it in the Middle Jurassic, a period when dinosaurs ruled both land and sea, but when mammal‑like creatures were still in their infancy. The Tiaojishan Formation is renowned for its exquisitely preserved feathered dinosaurs and early birds, yet mammalian fossils from this horizon remain scarce. This new find therefore fills a crucial gap in the fossil record, demonstrating that mammaliaforms were not merely passive by‑standers but active participants in the ecosystems of the time. The presence of aquatic adaptations also raises questions about the availability of freshwater habitats in the region and how these may have served as refuges or feeding grounds for early mammals.

Evolutionary biologists see the specimen as a vivid illustration of convergent evolution, where unrelated lineages independently develop similar solutions to environmental challenges. The broad, muscular tail mirrors the evolution of swimming tails in reptiles such as ichthyosaurs and later in mammals like sirenians, while the reinforced hyoid echoes the structural changes seen in modern cetaceans that enable sophisticated feeding strategies. This parallel suggests that the selective pressures of water—efficient locomotion, prey capture, and predator avoidance—have repeatedly shaped vertebrate anatomy across deep time.

Looking ahead, the find opens new avenues for research into the early diversification of mammals. Further excavation in the Tiaojishan and comparable Jurassic deposits could uncover additional specimens that clarify whether aquatic habits were isolated experiments or part of a broader, yet undocumented, trend among early mammaliaforms. Moreover, advanced imaging techniques, such as synchrotron tomography, may reveal soft‑tissue impressions or micro‑anatomical details that shed light on the animal’s musculature and respiratory adaptations. As paleontologists continue to piece together the mosaic of mammalian ancestry, this tiny, swimming predecessor stands as a reminder that the story of mammals is far more intricate—and far more aquatic—than previously imagined.
